domain.title: Databases & Storage
domain.tag: SQL · storage engines · transactions · query processing · the modern stack
domain.why: Every app you've ever used stores data somewhere, and eventually that storage becomes the whole bottleneck — for speed, for correctness, for what's even possible to build. Databases are where distributed systems, algorithms, and performance all show up in one place you can actually poke at. Understanding them deeply is rarer than it should be, because most people treat a database as a box you just save things into.

sections.t: SQL, the language you actually type
sections.note: Every statement here was executed against PostgreSQL 16.13. Dialect differences are called out where they exist.

concepts.t: The order a SELECT is actually evaluated in

L0.body:
-- PostgreSQL 16. Written order is not evaluation order.
SELECT c.region, count(*) AS n  -- 5. select list: aliases born here
FROM   customer c               -- 1. FROM
JOIN   orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id   -- 2. JOIN
WHERE  o.status = 'paid'        -- 3. WHERE: alias n does not exist yet
GROUP  BY c.region              -- 4. GROUP BY
HAVING count(*) > 2             -- 4b. HAVING: filters groups
ORDER  BY n DESC                -- 6. ORDER BY: alias n is visible
LIMIT  5;                       -- 7. LIMIT

-- `WHERE n > 2` gives:  ERROR:  column "n" does not exist
L0.cloze:
SELECT c.region, count(*) AS n
FROM customer c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'   -- alias n is {{c1::not}} visible here
GROUP BY c.region
HAVING count(*) > 2       -- filters {{c2::groups}}, after aggregation
ORDER BY n DESC           -- alias n {{c3::is}} visible here
-- Order: FROM, {{c4::WHERE}}, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT

concepts.L1: Clauses are evaluated FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. The select list is fifth, which is why an alias defined there is visible to ORDER BY but not to WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING.
concepts.L2: WHERE and HAVING are not two spellings of the same filter. WHERE removes rows before grouping and can use an index; HAVING removes whole groups after aggregation and cannot. Moving a predicate between them changes the answer, not just the speed.
concepts.L3: The order falls out of what each clause consumes. FROM and JOIN produce a row stream; WHERE is a predicate over one row of that stream, so it runs while the stream still exists. GROUP BY then destroys the stream, replacing it with one row per group, so anything after it can only see grouped values or aggregates. HAVING is a predicate over a group. Only then does the select list get evaluated, which is the first moment an output alias exists as a name. ORDER BY and LIMIT operate on the finished result, so ORDER BY may use the alias. Postgres and MySQL both allow the alias in ORDER BY and GROUP BY as an extension; the standard allows it only in ORDER BY.

L4.prompt_tpl: A developer writes `SELECT total_cents / {div} AS dollars FROM orders WHERE dollars > 10;` against PostgreSQL and gets an error. Give the exact error and the two ways to fix it without a subquery.
L4.answer: ERROR: column "dollars" does not exist. WHERE is evaluated before the select list, so the alias has not been created. Fix by repeating the expression (`WHERE total_cents / 100 > 10`) or, better, by writing the predicate on the raw column (`WHERE total_cents > 1000`) so an index on total_cents remains usable.
L4.explanation: Repeating the expression works but `total_cents / 100 > 10` is not sargable against a plain B-tree index on total_cents; rewriting it as `total_cents > 1000` is. This is the practical reason the rule matters.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need only orders with status 'paid' counted per region. Compare `WHERE o.status = 'paid'` against `HAVING bool_and(o.status = 'paid')`. Which regions does each return, and which can use an index on orders(status)?
L4.answer: WHERE returns every region that has at least one paid order, counting only paid orders, and can use the index. HAVING keeps only regions where every order is paid, counts all their orders, and cannot use the index because the predicate is evaluated after grouping.
L4.explanation: This is the cleanest demonstration that WHERE and HAVING are semantically different operators, not stylistic alternatives. HAVING exists for predicates over aggregates; anything expressible on a single row belongs in WHERE.

concepts.t: Joins: what each one does to the row count

L0.body:
-- PostgreSQL 16. customer has 4 rows; 'di' has placed no orders.
SELECT c.name, count(o.id)
FROM customer c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY c.name;
--  ana | 1
--  bo  | 1
--  cy  | 2
--  di  | 0      <- preserved by the LEFT JOIN

-- Move the same predicate to WHERE and 'di' disappears entirely:
--   LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
--   WHERE o.status = 'paid'      -- NULL = 'paid' is UNKNOWN -> row dropped
L0.cloze:
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
-- a predicate in {{c1::ON}} filters before the outer rows are padded
-- the same predicate in {{c2::WHERE}} runs after, silently turning the
-- LEFT JOIN into an {{c3::INNER}} join
-- INNER JOIN row count = sum over matching keys of {{c4::left_n * right_n}}

concepts.L1: INNER keeps only matching pairs, LEFT keeps every left row padding non-matches with NULL, FULL keeps unmatched rows from both sides. A join is a filtered Cartesian product, so a duplicated key on both sides multiplies rows.
concepts.L2: Putting an outer join's filter in WHERE instead of ON converts it back into an inner join, because the NULL-padded rows fail the predicate under three-valued logic. The query still runs, still looks like a LEFT JOIN, and quietly returns fewer rows.
concepts.L3: The relational definition: form the Cartesian product, keep the pairs satisfying ON, then for an outer join add back every unmatched row from the preserved side with NULLs in the other side's columns. The order matters. ON is applied while the pairs exist; the NULL padding happens after; WHERE runs after that, so `WHERE o.status = 'paid'` compares 'paid' against a NULL, yields UNKNOWN, and discards the row. It is also why the row count is not bounded by either input: if three orders share a customer_id and two customers share it too, that key contributes six rows. An unnoticed one-to-many join is the commonest cause of a silently doubled sum.

L4.prompt_tpl: Table L has {ln} rows all with key = 7. Table R has {rn} rows all with key = 7, plus 3 rows with key = 9. How many rows does `L INNER JOIN R ON L.key = R.key` return, and how many does `L LEFT JOIN R ON L.key = R.key` return?
L4.answer: Both return ln*rn. INNER: ln*rn matching pairs. LEFT: every L row matches at least one R row, so no NULL padding is added and the count is identical. For ln=4, rn=5 that is 20; for ln=2, rn=3 it is 6.
L4.explanation: A LEFT JOIN only exceeds an INNER JOIN when some left row has zero matches. The R rows with key = 9 never appear in either result. The trap is assuming LEFT JOIN always returns at least as many rows as the left table has: it returns more when the right side has duplicates.

L4.prompt_tpl: `SELECT c.name, count(o.id) FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY c.name` is meant to list every customer with their paid-order count, including customers with none. It omits them. Why, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: The WHERE predicate is evaluated after NULL padding, so for a customer with no orders o.status is NULL and NULL = 'paid' is UNKNOWN, which WHERE discards. Move the predicate into the ON clause: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'`.
L4.explanation: `WHERE o.something IS NULL` is the one outer-join WHERE predicate that is safe, and it is the standard anti-join idiom. Every other predicate on the null-supplying side belongs in ON.

prereqs: The order a SELECT is actually evaluated in

L0.body:
-- PostgreSQL 16, exact output.
SELECT (NULL = NULL)        AS eq,      -- NULL  (not true)
       (NULL IS NULL)       AS isnull,  -- t
       (1 IN (2, NULL))     AS in3,     -- NULL
       (1 NOT IN (2, NULL)) AS notin3;  -- NULL

SELECT count(*), count(region) FROM customer;   -- 4 | 3

-- customer has 4 rows, one with region NULL:
SELECT count(*) FROM customer WHERE region NOT IN ('eu', NULL);  -- 0
SELECT count(*) FROM customer WHERE region NOT IN ('eu');        -- 2

concepts.L1: SQL predicates are three-valued: TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN. NULL means 'no value here', so any comparison with it yields UNKNOWN, and WHERE, ON and CHECK each keep only rows where the predicate is TRUE. NULL is not zero and not the empty string.
concepts.L2: `NOT IN` with a NULL anywhere in the list returns no rows at all, not the rows you expected. `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` expands to `x <> 1 AND x <> NULL`, whose second conjunct is UNKNOWN, so the whole thing is FALSE or UNKNOWN and never TRUE. `NOT EXISTS` has no such trap.
concepts.L3: `IN` is defined as a disjunction of equalities and `NOT IN` as a conjunction of inequalities. With a NULL present, `x <> NULL` is UNKNOWN for every x. UNKNOWN AND FALSE is FALSE; UNKNOWN AND TRUE is UNKNOWN. So the conjunction is never TRUE and the filter admits nothing. The measured case above shows it: `region NOT IN ('eu')` returns 2 rows, adding NULL to the list returns 0. CHECK constraints invert the rule and accept UNKNOWN, which is why `CHECK (qty >= 0)` does not reject a NULL qty. count(*) counts rows because it takes no argument; count(col) counts non-null values of that argument, and the gap between them is the standard null census.

L4.prompt_tpl: In PostgreSQL, a table has {n} rows and column c contains no NULLs, plus one extra row where c IS NULL. What does `SELECT count(*), count(c) FROM t` return, and what does `SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE c NOT IN (SELECT c FROM t)` return? Answer with the value of count(c).
L4.answer: count(*) is n+1 and count(c) is n. The NOT IN subquery returns 0 rows, because the subquery result contains a NULL, making every `c <> NULL` conjunct UNKNOWN.
L4.explanation: The second half is the classic production outage: an anti-join written with NOT IN against a nullable column silently returns nothing. The fix is NOT EXISTS, or adding `WHERE c IS NOT NULL` to the subquery.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must find rows where two nullable columns differ, treating NULL as a value so that (NULL, 5) counts as differing and (NULL, NULL) does not. Which predicate is correct: `a <> b`, `a IS DISTINCT FROM b`, or `coalesce(a,-1) <> coalesce(b,-1)`?
L4.answer: `a IS DISTINCT FROM b`
L4.explanation: `a <> b` yields UNKNOWN whenever either side is NULL, so it finds neither case. The coalesce trick works only if the sentinel can never occur in the data, which is a bug waiting for a -1. IS DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-aware comparison and is what the SQL standard defines for exactly this.

concepts.t: GROUP BY, HAVING, and what an aggregate can see

L0.body:
-- PostgreSQL 16. Grouping by the primary key licenses the other columns.
SELECT c.id, c.name, count(o.id)
FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id             -- c.name is functionally dependent on c.id
ORDER BY c.id;
--  1 | ana | 3     4 | di | 0    <- count(o.id) is 0, not 1

-- Without the PK in GROUP BY, Postgres refuses:
--   SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customer c GROUP BY c.name;
--   ERROR:  column "c.id" must appear in the GROUP BY clause
--           or be used in an aggregate function

concepts.L1: GROUP BY collapses the row stream into one row per distinct grouping value. Every select-list item must then be a grouping column, an aggregate, or provably determined by a grouped key. Aggregates skip NULLs; count(*) does not, because it has no argument.
concepts.L2: In a LEFT JOIN, `count(*)` and `count(right.col)` differ by exactly the unmatched rows: count(*) reports 1 for a customer with no orders, count(o.id) reports 0. Almost every 'why does this customer show one order' bug is this.
concepts.L3: Grouping is a partition of the input by the grouping expressions. A column that is not in the partition key has no single value within a group, so referencing it is meaningless; the standard rejects it. The exception is functional dependency: if you group by a primary key, every other column of that table has exactly one value per group, and Postgres, DB2 and MySQL 5.7+ with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY all accept it. MySQL without that flag silently picks an arbitrary row's value, which is where the 'MySQL returns wrong data' folklore comes from. Aggregates other than count(*) ignore NULL inputs, so avg over a column with nulls divides by the non-null count, not the row count.

L4.prompt_tpl: A customer has placed {k} orders. A second customer has placed none. The query is `SELECT c.id, count(*), count(o.id) FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id`. Give both counts for each customer. Answer with count(*) for the first customer.
L4.answer: For the first customer both are k. For the second, count(*) is 1 and count(o.id) is 0. The LEFT JOIN emits one NULL-padded row for the customer with no orders; count(*) counts that row, count(o.id) skips it because o.id is NULL.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common aggregation bug in application code. The rule: in an outer join, always count a column from the null-supplying side, never count(*).

L4.prompt_tpl: PostgreSQL accepts `SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customer c GROUP BY c.id` but rejects `... GROUP BY c.name`. Explain the rule that distinguishes them in one sentence.
L4.answer: c.id is the primary key, so c.name is functionally dependent on it and has exactly one value per group; c.name is not a key, so several distinct c.id values can share a name and the select list would have no single value to report.
L4.explanation: The standard calls this functional dependency and permits exactly this relaxation. It is why grouping by a surrogate primary key is almost always the right shape for a per-entity aggregate query.

L0.body:
-- PostgreSQL 16, exact output. Ties expose the default frame.
WITH v(x) AS (VALUES (10),(10),(20))
SELECT x,
       sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY x)                          AS range_default,
       sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY x ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_frame
FROM v;
--  x  | range_default | rows_frame
--  10 |            20 |         10
--  10 |            20 |         20
--  20 |            40 |         40

SELECT id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                              ORDER BY placed_at DESC) AS rn
FROM orders;
L0.cloze:
sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY x)   -- default frame is {{c1::RANGE}} BETWEEN
                           -- UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW,
                           -- which includes all {{c2::peers}} (ties)
sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY x {{c3::ROWS}} UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) -- true running total
-- A window function cannot be referenced in {{c4::WHERE}}; wrap it in a
-- subquery or CTE and filter outside.

concepts.L1: A window function computes over a set of rows related to the current row and returns one value per input row, so nothing is collapsed. OVER defines the partition, the ordering within it, and the frame of rows the function sees.
concepts.L2: With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, which includes every row that ties on the ordering key. On duplicate values a 'running total' silently jumps by the whole tie group. Write ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING when you mean a per-row running total.
concepts.L3: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING but before ORDER BY and LIMIT, which is why the result cannot be filtered in WHERE and why an aggregate can be an argument to a window function but not the reverse. The frame comes in two units. ROWS counts physical rows, so the frame ends exactly at the current row. RANGE counts by the value of the ORDER BY expression, so rows with an equal value are peers and enter the frame together. The measured example makes the gap visible: both 10s report 20 under RANGE and 10 then 20 under ROWS. row_number ignores ties, rank leaves gaps after them, dense_rank does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: Values are {vals}, ordered ascending. Give the output of `sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY x)` and of `sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY x ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` for each row, in order.
L4.answer: For (5,5,7): RANGE gives 10, 10, 17; ROWS gives 5, 10, 17. For (1,2,2,4): RANGE gives 1, 5, 5, 9; ROWS gives 1, 3, 5, 9. RANGE lumps peers together and reports the group total to every peer; ROWS accumulates one row at a time.
L4.explanation: Both frames agree on the last row of every peer group and on the final total; they disagree only inside a tie. This is why the bug is so hard to spot on test data with no duplicates.

L4.prompt_tpl: `SELECT id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at DESC) AS rn FROM orders WHERE rn = 1` fails with 'column rn does not exist'. Explain why and rewrite it to return each customer's most recent order.
L4.answer: Window functions are computed after WHERE, so rn does not exist when WHERE runs. Wrap it: `SELECT * FROM (SELECT id, customer_id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at DESC) AS rn FROM orders) s WHERE rn = 1;` In PostgreSQL, `DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id, placed_at DESC` is a shorter equivalent.
L4.explanation: DISTINCT ON is Postgres-only. The subquery form is portable and is the standard top-N-per-group idiom. MySQL 8+ and SQL Server accept the same subquery shape.

L0.cloze:
WITH RECURSIVE t(n) AS (
    SELECT 1                          -- the {{c1::anchor}} term
  UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM t WHERE n < 5   -- the {{c2::recursive}} term
)
-- UNION (without ALL) additionally {{c3::deduplicates}}, which is what
-- stops a cyclic graph walk from looping forever.
-- Postgres 12+ inlines a CTE unless you write {{c4::MATERIALIZED}}.

concepts.L1: A common table expression names a subquery for the duration of one statement. WITH RECURSIVE adds a self-reference: an anchor term runs once, then the recursive term runs repeatedly against only the rows the previous iteration produced, until it yields none.
concepts.L2: Before Postgres 12 a CTE was an unconditional optimisation fence: predicates were never pushed into it, so wrapping a query in WITH could turn an index scan into a full scan. Since 12 it inlines single-use non-recursive CTEs, and MATERIALIZED is how you ask for the old behaviour back.
concepts.L3: The evaluation is a fixpoint iteration, not true recursion. Postgres keeps a working table holding the previous iteration's output; each step evaluates the recursive term against exactly that table, appends the result to the output, and replaces the working table with it. Iteration stops when a step produces zero rows, which is why the termination condition must live in the recursive term. UNION ALL appends blindly; UNION deduplicates against everything emitted so far, which is what makes a graph traversal terminate on a cycle. There is no depth limit, so a wrong predicate is an unbounded loop that consumes disk until it fills.

L4.prompt_tpl: `WITH RECURSIVE t(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + {step} FROM t WHERE n < {lim}) SELECT count(*), max(n), sum(n) FROM t;` Give all three values. Answer with the count.
L4.answer: The sequence is 1, 1+step, 1+2*step, ... and a row is produced while the previous n < lim. Count is floor((lim-1)/step) + 2 when (lim-1) is not a multiple of step, else (lim-1)/step + 1... compute directly: for step=1, lim=5 the rows are 1,2,3,4,5 so count=5, max=5, sum=15. For step=2, lim=10 the rows are 1,3,5,7,9,11 so count=6, max=11, sum=36. For step=3, lim=10 the rows are 1,4,7,10 so count=4, max=10, sum=22.
L4.explanation: The subtlety is the off-by-one: the guard tests the row that already exists, so one row beyond the limit is always emitted. With step=2 and lim=10 the last row is 11, not 9. Trace the working table rather than reasoning about the limit.

L4.prompt_tpl: A recursive CTE walking a `follows(a, b)` graph with UNION ALL never finishes on production data but is fine in tests. Name the cause and the two standard fixes.
L4.answer: The production graph contains a cycle, and UNION ALL never deduplicates so the traversal revisits nodes forever. Fix by using UNION instead of UNION ALL, or by carrying a path array and adding `WHERE NOT b = ANY(path)` plus a depth guard such as `WHERE depth < 100`.
L4.explanation: UNION alone is enough for a pure reachability query. The path-array form is needed when you must report the path, or when the same node may legitimately be visited by different routes.

concepts.t: Correlated subqueries: EXISTS, IN, and the NOT IN trap

L0.body:
-- PostgreSQL 16. Correlated: the inner query references the outer row.
SELECT c.name
FROM customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.id      -- the correlation
                AND o.total_cents > 5000);

-- Anti-join. NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are not equivalent when the column
-- is nullable. customer has 4 rows, one of them with region NULL:
SELECT count(*) FROM customer
 WHERE region NOT IN (SELECT region FROM customer);      -- 0
SELECT count(*) FROM customer WHERE region NOT IN ('eu');  -- 2

concepts.L1: A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it is logically re-evaluated once per outer row. EXISTS asks only whether the inner query yields at least one row; its select list is never evaluated, which is why `SELECT 1` is idiomatic.
concepts.L2: NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are not interchangeable. If the NOT IN subquery produces even one NULL, the predicate can never be TRUE and the query returns zero rows. NOT EXISTS has no null semantics at all: it is a pure emptiness test.
concepts.L3: Logically a correlated subquery is a nested loop, and a naive engine executes it that way at cost proportional to the outer row count. Real optimisers do not: Postgres, Oracle and SQL Server decorrelate EXISTS and IN into semi-joins and NOT EXISTS into anti-joins, then choose hash or merge strategies for them, so the correlated form usually plans identically to the explicit join. The exception is a subquery in the select list, or one containing LIMIT or a volatile function, which cannot be decorrelated and does run per row. The NOT IN hazard is separate and semantic: it means NOT (x = ANY s), and a NULL in s makes that comparison UNKNOWN, so the negation is never TRUE.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want customers with no orders. Rank these three for correctness and plan quality: (a) `NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`, (b) `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`, (c) `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL`.
L4.answer: (b) and (c) are both correct and both plan as an anti-join; prefer (b) as it states the intent and cannot be broken by a later added predicate. (a) is correct only if orders.customer_id is NOT NULL, and silently returns zero rows if it is nullable and any row has a NULL. If the column is declared NOT NULL, Postgres can plan (a) as an anti-join too.
L4.explanation: The declared nullability of the column is what makes the difference, which is why NOT NULL constraints are a query-planning feature and not only a data-integrity one.

L4.prompt_tpl: `orders.customer_id` is nullable and exactly {k} rows have it NULL. `SELECT count(*) FROM customer WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);` The table has 4 customers, 3 of whom have orders. What is the count?
L4.answer: 0. As soon as the subquery yields at least one NULL, every `id <> NULL` conjunct is UNKNOWN, so the predicate is never TRUE and no rows qualify. The answer is 0 for any k >= 1; it would be 1 only if k = 0.
L4.explanation: The result does not depend on how many NULLs there are, only on whether there is at least one. That is what makes this bug intermittent: it appears the first time a NULL lands in the column, long after the query was written.

-- `actual rows=` is the truth. A large ratio between them is the
-- root cause of most bad plans.

-- rows multiplied by {{c4::loops}}.
-- Heap Fetches: 0 means the scan was {{c5::index-only}}.

concepts.L1: EXPLAIN prints the chosen plan and its cost estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and adds measured row counts, timings and loop counts. BUFFERS adds pages hit in the buffer pool versus read from storage.
concepts.L2: Under a nested loop, `actual rows` and `actual time` are per iteration, not totals: a line reading `actual rows=3 loops=20000` did 60000 rows of work. Reading the inner number as a total is why people conclude a nested loop is cheap when it is the thing burning the query.
concepts.L3: The value of ANALYZE is the estimate-versus-actual comparison, because the optimiser's one real weakness is cardinality. Read the plan bottom-up and inside-out, find the deepest node whose estimated rows differ from actual by more than an order of magnitude, and fix that node: its parent's algorithm choice was made from the wrong number. BUFFERS converts the abstract cost into pages, which is the unit the buffer pool and the disk actually deal in. The two plans above are the same predicate on the same index: the first touches 8 pages because every column it needs is in the index, the second touches 1000 heap pages because it needs column v and the matching rows are scattered.

L4.prompt_tpl: A plan node reads `Nested Loop ... -> Index Scan on child (actual rows={r} loops={l})`. How many child rows were actually produced in total, and what single number should you check first to decide whether the nested loop was the right choice? Answer with the total number of child rows produced.

L4.explanation: A nested loop is correct when the outer side is genuinely small; it degrades linearly when the estimate was low. This is the single most common plan regression after statistics drift, and the loops multiplier is where you see it.

The second needed a column the index does not carry, so each of the 1000 matching rows required a heap visit, and because the rows are physically scattered those were 1000 distinct pages.
L4.explanation: This is the entire argument for covering indexes stated as a measurement: adding one column to the index removed 1000 random page reads. It also shows why physical correlation between index order and heap order matters so much.

concepts.t: Transaction control in SQL: SAVEPOINT, FOR UPDATE, ON CONFLICT

L0.cloze:
SAVEPOINT s1;  ...  {{c1::ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT}} s1;
-- without this, any error aborts the whole transaction and every
-- later statement fails with 'current transaction is {{c2::aborted}}'
SELECT ... {{c3::FOR UPDATE}};   -- takes a row lock held until COMMIT
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = inv.qty + {{c4::EXCLUDED}}.qty
-- MySQL spells the same thing INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE,
-- and the SQL standard spells it {{c5::MERGE}}.

concepts.L1: BEGIN opens a transaction; COMMIT makes every change durable and visible at once; ROLLBACK discards all of it. SAVEPOINT marks a point you can partially roll back to. FOR UPDATE takes a row lock now, so a later read-modify-write cannot be lost.
concepts.L2: In PostgreSQL any error aborts the entire transaction: every subsequent statement fails until you ROLLBACK or return to a SAVEPOINT. MySQL does not do this, so code ported from MySQL that ignores a duplicate-key error works there and dies here.
concepts.L3: The lost-update problem is why FOR UPDATE exists. Under READ COMMITTED two sessions read qty = 5, each compute 4, each write 4, both commit, and one decrement vanishes; the database has done nothing wrong, since neither transaction read a value the other wrote. FOR UPDATE serialises the pair at the row. ON CONFLICT collapses the read-then-insert-or-update race into one statement performed atomically against the unique index, so no window exists between check and write. EXCLUDED is the proposed row that lost; the table name gives the existing row. Savepoints are subtransactions with their own transaction ids, which is why one per loop iteration is a known performance problem.

L4.prompt_tpl: Application code does `SELECT qty FROM inv WHERE sku = 'a'`, computes `qty - {d}` in the application, then `UPDATE inv SET qty = <computed>`. Under READ COMMITTED with two concurrent workers, what goes wrong and give two distinct fixes.
L4.answer: A lost update: both read the same qty, both write a value derived from it, and one decrement is lost. Fix 1: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` so the second reader blocks until the first commits. Fix 2: do the arithmetic in the database with `UPDATE inv SET qty = qty - d WHERE sku = 'a'`, which reads and writes atomically under the row lock the UPDATE already takes. Fix 3: run at REPEATABLE READ, where the second write raises a serialization failure the application must retry.
L4.explanation: The in-database arithmetic fix is the cheapest and is preferred where the computation permits it. FOR UPDATE is needed when the computation cannot be expressed in SQL. REPEATABLE READ converts the silent corruption into a visible error, which still requires retry logic.

L4.prompt_tpl: In PostgreSQL: `BEGIN; INSERT INTO inv VALUES ('a', {q}); -- duplicate key error` then `SELECT count(*) FROM inv; COMMIT;`. What does the SELECT return?
L4.answer: Nothing: it fails with 'ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block', and the COMMIT behaves as a ROLLBACK. Wrapping the INSERT in a SAVEPOINT and issuing ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after the error would let the SELECT run.
L4.explanation: This is a genuine dialect difference. MySQL and Oracle leave the transaction usable after a statement error; PostgreSQL does not. Client libraries such as psycopg emulate the savepoint dance for you when you use nested transaction blocks.

-- PostgreSQL 16. Three different claims about uniqueness.
CREATE TABLE employee (
  id      bigserial PRIMARY KEY,   -- surrogate key
  email   text NOT NULL UNIQUE,    -- natural candidate key
  dept_id int  NOT NULL REFERENCES dept(id),
  desk    text,
  UNIQUE (dept_id, desk)           -- composite candidate key;
);                                 -- a NULL desk repeats freely

-- The functional dependencies asserted above:
--   id              -> email, dept_id, desk
--   email           -> id, dept_id, desk
--   (dept_id, desk) -> id, email
-- UNIQUE IS a declared functional dependency.
L0.cloze:
id bigserial PRIMARY KEY    -- a {{c1::surrogate}} key: no business meaning
email text NOT NULL UNIQUE  -- a {{c2::candidate}} key drawn from the data
UNIQUE (dept_id, desk)      -- a {{c3::composite}} candidate key
-- Written X -> Y, "X {{c4::functionally determines}} Y": for any two rows
-- agreeing on X, they must agree on Y.
-- In SQL, UNIQUE lets multiple rows share a {{c5::NULL}}, so a nullable
-- unique column is not a key in the relational sense.

concepts.L1: A functional dependency X determines Y means any two rows agreeing on X must agree on Y. A candidate key is a minimal set of columns that determines every other column; the primary key is the candidate key you chose to reference from elsewhere.
concepts.L2: SQL's UNIQUE is weaker than a relational key: it permits unlimited NULLs, since NULL is never equal to NULL. `UNIQUE (dept_id, desk)` with desk NULL constrains nothing at all, which is how duplicate 'unique' rows appear in production.
concepts.L3: Every normalisation rule is stated in terms of functional dependencies, so you cannot reason about schema design without naming them first. Determine them from the business rules, not from the current data: an FD that happens to hold in today's rows but is not guaranteed is exactly the assumption that breaks. Minimality matters, because a superkey that is not minimal carries a redundant column into every foreign key referencing it. The surrogate-versus-natural choice is a trade: a surrogate never changes and stays narrow, so joins and indexes are cheap, but it does not prevent duplicate business entities - which is why you declare the natural key as UNIQUE alongside it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A table has columns (order_id, line_no, sku, qty, unit_price, order_date). Given the FDs order_id determines order_date, and (order_id, line_no) determines sku, qty, unit_price, name the candidate key and say which non-key column is stored redundantly.
L4.answer: The candidate key is (order_id, line_no). order_date is redundant: it depends on order_id alone, which is a proper subset of the key, so it is repeated once per line of the order and can disagree with itself after a partial update.
L4.explanation: A non-key column depending on part of a composite key is exactly a second-normal-form violation. The fix is to move order_date into an orders table keyed by order_id.

L4.prompt_tpl: A schema declares `desk text, dept_id int NOT NULL, UNIQUE (dept_id, desk)` and the team is surprised to find {n} rows for department 3 all with desk NULL. Explain, and give the PostgreSQL 15+ fix.
L4.answer: UNIQUE compares with = under three-valued logic, so two NULL desks are never equal and never conflict; the constraint permits unlimited such rows. PostgreSQL 15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (dept_id, desk)`, which treats NULLs as equal. The portable alternative is a NOT NULL column with an explicit sentinel, or a partial unique index plus a separate one for the null case.
L4.explanation: This is the SQL standard's behaviour, not a Postgres quirk; MySQL and Oracle do the same. NULLS NOT DISTINCT is a Postgres 15+ extension of the standard's optional feature.

concepts.t: Normal forms, with the reason instead of the ritual

L0.cloze:
-- 1NF: every column holds one {{c1::atomic}} value; no repeating groups.
-- 2NF: no non-key column depends on {{c2::part}} of a composite key.
-- 3NF: no non-key column depends on another {{c3::non-key}} column.
-- BCNF: every determinant is a {{c4::candidate key}}.
-- The point of all four is to eliminate {{c5::redundancy}}, because
-- redundancy is what makes update, insert and delete anomalies possible.

concepts.L1: Normal forms are anomaly-elimination rules, not style. Each higher form removes one shape of redundancy: 2NF removes dependence on part of a key, 3NF removes dependence on a non-key column, BCNF removes dependence on any non-candidate-key determinant.
concepts.L2: The forms are not about saving space. They are about making a fact storable in exactly one place, so that no update can leave two copies disagreeing. A denormalised schema is not wrong, but it moves the consistency obligation from the database into every writer.
concepts.L3: Take the table above. cust_city is stored once per order line, so a customer with 40 lines has the city 40 times. Nothing in SQL forces those 40 copies to agree: an UPDATE that misses a row leaves the database self-contradictory, and no constraint can detect it, because the constraint would have to compare rows rather than validate one. Decomposing stores each fact once and lets a foreign key carry it, so the anomaly becomes unrepresentable. The practical stopping point is BCNF: 3NF is always achievable while preserving all dependencies, BCNF sometimes is not, and 4NF and 5NF address multivalued and join dependencies that are rare in transactional schemas.

L4.prompt_tpl: `invoice(inv_id PK, cust_id, cust_email, total)` where cust_id determines cust_email. Name the highest normal form it satisfies, name the violated dependency, and state one anomaly with a concrete {n}-row example.
L4.answer: It satisfies 2NF but not 3NF: cust_id is not a key yet determines cust_email, a transitive dependency inv_id -> cust_id -> cust_email. Anomaly: a customer with n invoices has their email stored n times; changing it must update all n rows atomically, and any partial update leaves two different emails for one customer with no constraint able to notice.
L4.explanation: 2NF is satisfied because the key is a single column, so no partial dependency is possible. That is why single-column keys jump straight from 1NF to the 3NF question.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give the one-sentence difference between 3NF and BCNF, and a schema where they differ.
L4.answer: 3NF permits a non-key column to determine part of a candidate key; BCNF forbids any determinant that is not a whole candidate key. Classic example: `enrol(student, course, teacher)` where (student, course) and (student, teacher) are both candidate keys and teacher determines course. It is in 3NF because course is a key attribute, but teacher is a determinant and not a candidate key, so it is not in BCNF.
L4.explanation: This is the case where BCNF decomposition loses the dependency (student, course) determines teacher, which cannot then be enforced by a key constraint. That trade is why 3NF is sometimes deliberately kept.

concepts.t: Constraints are the only thing that makes the data true

  -- insert mutually-referencing rows in any order
EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH {{c4::&&}})
  -- generalises UNIQUE from equality to any operator; this one forbids
  -- {{c5::overlapping}} bookings for the same room

concepts.L1: A constraint is an invariant the engine enforces on every writer, forever, including the ones written after you leave. NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY and EXCLUDE are declarative claims about what is true, checked at statement end or at commit.
concepts.L2: CHECK rejects only predicates that evaluate to FALSE, so `CHECK (qty >= 0)` accepts a NULL qty: UNKNOWN is not FALSE. Constraints on nullable columns need an explicit NOT NULL or an `IS NOT NULL AND ...` form to mean what they look like they mean.
concepts.L3: The argument for pushing invariants into the database is that application checks are per-writer and the database is shared. A check in one service is not enforced against the migration script, the psql session, the backfill job or the second service written next year. Bailis's 'Feral Concurrency Control' measured this across popular Rails applications and found the ORM validations they relied on to be racy under concurrency in exactly the cases a unique index would have caught. Constraints are also a planning input: NOT NULL enables anti-join rewrites, UNIQUE tells the optimiser a join yields at most one row per key, and a CHECK can let a partition be pruned outright.

L4.prompt_tpl: `CREATE TABLE t (qty int, CHECK (qty >= {lo}))` then `INSERT INTO t VALUES (NULL)` succeeds. Explain why and give the fix.
L4.answer: A CHECK constraint rejects a row only when the predicate evaluates to FALSE. With a NULL, `qty >= lo` evaluates to UNKNOWN, which the standard treats as satisfying the constraint. Fix by declaring the column NOT NULL, or by writing the constraint as `CHECK (qty IS NOT NULL AND qty >= lo)`.
L4.explanation: This is the opposite convention from WHERE, which keeps only TRUE. The asymmetry is deliberate in the standard and it catches almost everyone once.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service enforces 'one active subscription per user' by reading the table, finding none active, then inserting. Two requests arrive {ms} milliseconds apart. What happens, and what single DDL statement makes the invariant actually hold?
L4.answer: Both reads see no active subscription, both insert, and the user ends with two. The check-then-act is not atomic and no isolation level below SERIALIZABLE stops it, because neither transaction wrote what the other read. `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON subscription (user_id) WHERE status = 'active';` - a partial unique index - makes the second insert fail with a constraint violation the application can handle.
L4.explanation: This is Bailis's feral concurrency control in one example: the invariant was real, the enforcement was in the wrong place. A partial unique index is the Postgres spelling; MySQL needs a generated column plus a unique index on it.

-- PostgreSQL 16. Three ways to buy read speed with write cost.
-- 1. Materialised view: stale until refreshed, refreshable online.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW region_totals AS
  SELECT c.region, sum(o.total_cents) AS cents
  FROM customer c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  GROUP BY c.region;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON region_totals (region);  -- CONCURRENTLY needs it
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY region_totals;

-- 2. Generated column: derived, always consistent, costs write CPU.
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_dollars numeric
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (total_cents / 100.0) STORED;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... ;  -- data is {{c1::stale}} until REFRESH
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW {{c2::CONCURRENTLY}} v;  -- needs a UNIQUE index,
                                    -- and does not block readers
GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) {{c3::STORED}}  -- recomputed on every write

-- a {{c5::write}} cost plus an obligation to keep copies consistent.

concepts.L2: The cost is not the extra bytes, it is that a second writer now exists for the same fact. A counter column updated by trigger turns every insert into a write to one shared row, which serialises concurrent inserts on that row's lock and can be slower overall than the aggregate you replaced.

The pattern pays when the aggregate spans far more rows than the request touches and reads greatly outnumber writes. Rank the mechanisms by how much consistency they keep: a generated STORED column is always correct because the engine derives it inside the same statement; a materialised view is exactly as stale as its refresh interval, fine for a dashboard and wrong for a balance check; a trigger-maintained counter is correct only if every writer goes through the trigger and its row lock is affordable.

L4.prompt_tpl: A counter column is maintained by an AFTER INSERT trigger doing `UPDATE stats SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = 1`. Inserts arrive at {rate} per second and each UPDATE holds the row lock for {us} microseconds. What is the maximum sustainable insert rate through that single row, and is the workload feasible? Answer with the maximum sustainable insert rate through the single row.
L4.answer: One row can absorb at most 1/(us*1e-6) updates per second: 1/50e-6 = 20000 per second, and 1/200e-6 = 5000 per second. Feasible when rate is below that ceiling; at rate 30000 with us=50 it is not, and lock waits will grow without bound. The standard fix is sharding the counter across k rows and summing on read.
L4.explanation: The ceiling is set by the serialised critical section, not by throughput of the table. This is the arithmetic that decides whether a counter column is an optimisation or a bottleneck, and it is the same reasoning as any single hot key.

L4.prompt_tpl: A dashboard shows per-region revenue, refreshed by humans every few minutes, over a 50-million-row orders table. Choose between a materialised view refreshed every 5 minutes, a trigger-maintained summary table, and just adding an index. Justify in two sentences.
L4.answer: The materialised view: the consumer tolerates minutes of staleness by construction, the refresh cost is paid once per interval rather than once per write, and it adds no lock contention on the insert path. A trigger-maintained table pays on every one of the writes to buy freshness nobody needs, and an index alone cannot avoid aggregating 50 million rows per view.
L4.explanation: Match the staleness of the mechanism to the staleness the consumer already accepts. The trigger is right only when a reader needs the number to be exact at read time, such as an inventory or balance check.

-- PostgreSQL 16 via pageinspect. Heap table 'orders', 9 rows, page 0.
SELECT lower, upper, special, pagesize FROM page_header(get_raw_page('orders',0));
--  lower | upper | special | pagesize
--     60 |  7616 |    8192 |     8192

SELECT lp, lp_off, lp_len FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('orders',0)) LIMIT 3;
--  lp | lp_off | lp_len
--   1 |   8128 |     61
--   2 |   8064 |     61
--   3 |   8000 |     61

-- lower = 24-byte page header + 9 line pointers * 4 bytes = 60
-- upper = 8192 - 9 tuples * 64 bytes (61 rounded up to MAXALIGN) = 7616
-- free space = upper - lower = 7556 bytes
L0.cloze:
-- A slotted page grows the {{c1::line pointer}} array from the low end and
-- the tuples from the {{c2::high}} end; free space is the gap between them.
-- lower = 24 + 4 * n_items ;  upper = pagesize - sum of aligned tuple sizes
-- A row's address, its {{c3::ctid}}, is (page, line pointer index) - which
-- means the tuple can be {{c4::moved}} within the page without changing it.
-- Freeing a tuple leaves a {{c5::dead}} line pointer, which is why VACUUM
-- reclaims space but not always the item-pointer slots.

concepts.L1: A page is the unit of I/O, 8 KB in Postgres and 16 KB in InnoDB by default. A slotted page stores a header, then an array of small line pointers growing upward, then variable-length tuples packed downward from the end, with free space in the middle.
concepts.L2: The indirection is the point. An index entry stores the line-pointer slot, not a byte offset, so the engine can compact a page and move tuples without touching any index. Change the slot number and every index would have to be rewritten.
concepts.L3: Variable-length rows make the naive layout impossible: you cannot address the k-th row by multiplication, and deleting one leaves a hole. The slotted layout solves both. The line-pointer array is fixed-width, so slot k is at a computed offset, and it holds the tuple's current position, so compaction is a page-local operation. This is what makes Postgres's HOT updates work: a new row version placed on the same page can be reached by redirecting the old line pointer, so no index needs updating at all. The numbers above are exact and worth reproducing: 24-byte header, 4 bytes per pointer, and MAXALIGN rounding each tuple up to a multiple of 8, which is why 61-byte tuples occupy 64.

L4.prompt_tpl: A PostgreSQL 8192-byte page holds {n} tuples whose raw length is {len} bytes each. Give lower, upper and the free space, given a 24-byte header, 4-byte line pointers, and MAXALIGN of 8. Answer with the free space in bytes.
L4.answer: aligned = 8*ceil(len/8). lower = 24 + 4n. upper = 8192 - n*aligned. free = upper - lower. For n=9, len=61: aligned 64, lower 60, upper 7616, free 7556. For n=100, len=61: lower 424, upper 1792, free 1368. For n=9, len=40: aligned 40, lower 60, upper 7832, free 7772.
L4.explanation: The formula is the whole concept. Note that each row costs 4 bytes of line pointer on top of its aligned size, so the effective per-row overhead is alignment padding plus 4, which is why very narrow rows waste a surprising fraction of a page.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does an index entry point at a line-pointer slot rather than at a byte offset within the page? Give the operation this makes cheap.
L4.answer: Because tuples move. Compacting a page to reclaim space left by dead tuples slides the live ones toward the end of the page; if indexes held byte offsets, every one of them would have to be rewritten. With a slot number, the engine updates the line pointer in place and no index changes. It also enables HOT chains, where an updated row version on the same page is reached through the old slot.
L4.explanation: This is the same indirection idea as a page table or a handle table in a garbage collector: one level of indirection converts a global rewrite into a local one.

-- PostgreSQL 16, measured. 1,000,000 rows, index on (k int4, id int8).
SELECT tree_level, internal_pages, leaf_pages, avg_leaf_density
FROM pgstatindex('t_k_id');
--  tree_level | internal_pages | leaf_pages | avg_leaf_density
--           2 |             20 |       3832 |            90.03

-- 1,000,000 / 3832 = 261 entries per leaf.
-- Entry: 8-byte IndexTuple header + int4 + 4 pad + int8 = 24,
--        plus a 4-byte line pointer = 28 bytes.
-- Usable: 8192 - 24 page header - 16 btree special = 8152.
-- 8152 * 0.90 / 28 = 262.  Matches.
-- Height 3: root -> 20 internal -> 3832 leaves.
L0.cloze:
-- fanout f = usable_page_bytes / bytes_per_entry
-- height h = ceil( log_f( N ) ) levels
-- A point lookup costs h page reads, of which the top {{c1::h-1}} are
-- almost always in the {{c2::buffer pool}}.
-- Doubling N adds {{c3::log_f(2)}} levels - which for f = 200 is about
-- one level per {{c4::200x}} growth. This is why B+ trees stay shallow.
-- Postgres stores {{c5::no}} data in internal nodes; keys are separators only.

concepts.L1: Fanout is how many child pointers fit in one page: usable page bytes divided by entry size. Height is the log of the row count in base fanout. With a 200-way fanout, a billion rows fit in four levels, so any lookup is at most four page reads.
concepts.L2: Fanout is set by key width, not by row width, which is why a wide composite or text key is expensive twice: it lowers fanout, raising height, and it makes every internal node comparison longer. Halving key size can remove a level from a large index.
concepts.L3: The reason the B+ tree beat every alternative on disk is that it makes the base of the logarithm the page size. A binary tree over a billion keys is 30 levels and therefore 30 random reads; a 200-way tree is 4. Each level multiplies capacity by the fanout, so height is the ceiling of log base f of N. The measured index above shows the real numbers: 28-byte entries, 8152 usable bytes, 90 percent fill, 262 entries per leaf, 3 levels for a million rows. In practice only the leaf read misses cache, because the root and the single internal level are 21 pages together and stay resident.

L4.prompt_tpl: An index has {N} entries, a fanout of {f}, and internal levels fully cached. How many levels does the tree have, and how many uncached page reads does one point lookup cost, ignoring the heap fetch? Answer with the number of levels.
L4.answer: levels = ceil(log_f(N)). For N=1e9, f=200: log200(1e9) = 9/2.301 = 3.91, so 4 levels. For N=1e9, f=50: 9/1.699 = 5.30, so 6 levels. For N=1e6, f=200: 6/2.301 = 2.61, so 3 levels. For N=1e6, f=50: 6/1.699 = 3.53, so 4 levels. Uncached reads is 1 in every case: only the leaf misses.
L4.explanation: The insight is that height barely moves and the cached-internal-levels assumption holds for any index whose non-leaf pages fit in the buffer pool, which is nearly all of them. Cutting fanout from 200 to 50 by using a fat key adds two levels and, more importantly, quadruples the index size.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague proposes replacing an int8 primary key with a 36-character UUID stored as text. Estimate the effect on leaf fanout in PostgreSQL, given an 8-byte IndexTuple header, 4-byte line pointer, MAXALIGN 8, and 8152 usable bytes per page.
L4.answer: int8: 8 + 8 = 16, aligned 16, plus 4 = 20 bytes per entry, about 407 entries per page at 100 percent fill and 366 at the default 90 percent fillfactor. UUID as text: 8 + 4 varlena header + 36 chars = 48, aligned 48, plus 4 = 52 bytes, about 156 entries at full and 141 at 90 percent. Fanout falls by roughly 2.6x and the index grows by the same factor. Storing it as the native uuid type is 8 + 16 = 24, aligned 24, plus 4 = 28 bytes, about 291 entries.
L4.explanation: Two costs compound: a bigger index that evicts more useful pages from the buffer pool, and random insertion order that also drives leaf density down toward 69 percent. The native uuid type recovers most of the first cost; UUIDv7 recovers the second.

--   2 | 3785 | 65.11

-- (b) CREATE INDEX built over the finished table (a sorted bulk load):
SELECT tree_level, leaf_pages, avg_leaf_density FROM pgstatindex('r2_id');
--   2 | 2733 | 90.06

-- Same data, same keys. 3785 vs 2733 leaf pages: 38% larger,
-- and 38% more of the buffer pool consumed to cache it.
L0.cloze:
-- Insert into a full leaf: allocate a new page, move {{c1::half}} the
-- entries into it, push a separator key up into the parent. If the parent
-- is also full it splits too, and a root split is the only way a B+ tree
-- grows {{c2::taller}}.
-- Under uniformly random inserts, steady-state occupancy converges to
-- ln 2, about {{c3::69}} percent.
-- Strictly increasing keys hit a special case: Postgres and InnoDB detect
-- rightmost-page inserts and split {{c4::asymmetrically}} instead of 50/50.

concepts.L1: Insertion into a full page splits it in half and promotes a separator key to the parent, propagating upward; a root split adds a level. Deletion may merge underfull siblings, though most engines defer or skip merging and simply leave pages partly empty.
concepts.L2: The 50/50 split is why a randomly-loaded B+ tree stabilises near 69 percent full, not 100. The measured pair above is the same data at 65 percent and 90 percent depending only on insertion order, a 38 percent size difference bought by rebuilding.
concepts.L3: Each split leaves two pages half full and each later insert into either fills it back toward the split point, so occupancy oscillates between one half and one, and the long-run average under uniform random keys is ln 2, about 0.693. The measurement above lands at 0.651 because Postgres also reserves a fillfactor margin; bulk building sorts first and packs to that fillfactor, hence 90 percent. Deletion is the asymmetric case: real engines rarely merge, because merging needs a latch on two siblings and their parent while a concurrent descent may be in flight, so they mark pages half-empty and reuse them. That is why an index over churning data keeps growing.

L4.prompt_tpl: An index leaf holds at most {cap} entries. You insert {n} keys in uniformly random order. Estimate the number of leaf pages, then the number if the same keys are bulk-loaded and packed to a 90 percent fillfactor. Answer with the estimated number of leaf pages under random insertion.
L4.answer: Random: pages = n / (cap * ln 2) = n / (0.693 * cap). For cap=367, n=1e6: 1e6/254 = 3932. For cap=367, n=1e7: 39320. For cap=100, n=1e6: 1e6/69.3 = 14430. Bulk at 90 percent: n / (0.9 * cap): 3027, 30270 and 11111 respectively. The random tree is about 30 percent larger.
L4.explanation: The measured Postgres numbers for cap=367, n=1e6 were 3785 random and 2733 bulk, within about 4 percent and 10 percent of these estimates. The estimate is good enough to decide whether a REINDEX is worth the buffer-pool savings.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why do PostgreSQL and InnoDB split the rightmost leaf page asymmetrically when keys arrive in increasing order, and what would a 50/50 split cost?
L4.answer: With monotonically increasing keys every insert lands on the rightmost page, so a 50/50 split immediately leaves a left half that will never receive another insert. The tree would settle at 50 percent occupancy and be twice the necessary size. Both engines detect the rightmost-insert pattern and split so that nearly all entries stay in the left page, packing it fully and leaving the new right page to receive the continuing stream.
L4.explanation: This is why an autoincrement or UUIDv7 primary key produces a much denser index than a random UUIDv4. It is also why the rightmost page becomes a latch hotspot in high-insert-rate workloads.

L0.cloze:
-- InnoDB: rows live in the {{c1::primary key}} B+ tree; a secondary index
-- leaf stores the {{c2::primary key value}}, not a physical address.
-- Consequence: a wide primary key inflates {{c3::every}} secondary index.
-- PostgreSQL: the heap is separate and every index stores a {{c4::ctid}}.
-- Consequence: an UPDATE that moves a row must update {{c5::every}} index,
-- unless the new version fits on the same page (a HOT update).

concepts.L1: A clustered index stores the rows themselves in index order, so the index is the table. A secondary index stores only keys plus a reference to the row: the primary key in InnoDB, a physical tuple id in PostgreSQL, and each choice pays somewhere different.
concepts.L2: InnoDB's logical row reference means a secondary lookup is always two B+ tree descents, but a row that moves costs nothing. Postgres's physical ctid means one descent, but every row relocation must update every index, which is precisely what HOT updates and fillfactor exist to avoid.
concepts.L3: This one choice explains most of the operational difference between MySQL and Postgres. In InnoDB a 36-byte UUID primary key adds 36 bytes to every entry of every secondary index and makes inserts land randomly in the clustered tree, so people learn to use an autoincrement key and keep the natural key in a secondary index. In Postgres the primary key is just another index, so its width is local, but the physical ctid means an ordinary UPDATE writes a new tuple and must add an entry to every index pointing at it. Heap-only tuples avoid that when the new version fits on the same page and no indexed column changed, which is why lowering fillfactor can cut index write traffic sharply.

L4.prompt_tpl: An InnoDB table has a {pk} primary key and {k} secondary indexes over {n} rows. Estimate the extra bytes the secondary indexes consume compared with an 8-byte BIGINT primary key, ignoring page overhead.
L4.answer: Extra per entry = pk_bytes - 8, times k indexes, times n rows. For pk=36 (CHAR(36) UUID), k=4, n=1e8: 28*4*1e8 = 11.2 GB. For pk=16 (BINARY(16)), k=4, n=1e8: 8*4*1e8 = 3.2 GB. For pk=36, k=2, n=1e7: 28*2*1e7 = 560 MB. For pk=16, k=2, n=1e7: 160 MB.
L4.explanation: The multiplier is the number of secondary indexes, which is why the cost is invisible on a two-index table and enormous on a heavily indexed one. Storing a UUID as BINARY(16) rather than CHAR(36) recovers most of it without changing the key.

L4.prompt_tpl: An UPDATE that changes only a non-indexed column is causing heavy index write traffic in PostgreSQL. Which single table setting is most likely to help, and why: raising fillfactor, lowering fillfactor, or adding an index on the updated column?
L4.answer: Lowering fillfactor
L4.explanation: Postgres can perform a heap-only tuple update, touching no index at all, when the new row version fits on the same page and no indexed column changed. Lowering fillfactor reserves free space on every page for exactly that. Raising it removes the space and makes HOT updates fail; adding an index makes the problem worse.
options: Adding an index on the updated column

L0.cloze:
CREATE INDEX ... ON t (k) {{c1::INCLUDE}} (v)
-- payload lives only in the {{c2::leaf}} pages, so internal-node fanout
-- is unchanged and the column cannot be used as a search key.
-- An {{c3::index-only}} scan reads no heap page at all - but Postgres must
-- still consult the {{c4::visibility map}}, so a table that has not been
-- VACUUMed recently reports nonzero {{c5::Heap Fetches}} and loses the win.

concepts.L1: A covering index contains every column a query needs, so the engine answers from the index and never reads the table. Postgres calls the resulting plan an index-only scan; INCLUDE adds payload columns to leaf pages without making them part of the key.
concepts.L2: In PostgreSQL an index-only scan is not guaranteed by a covering index. Visibility lives in the heap, so the engine checks the visibility map per page and falls back to a heap fetch for any page not marked all-visible. On a recently-written table it degrades silently to an ordinary index scan.
concepts.L3: The measurement above is the whole argument. Both queries match the same 1000 rows through the same index. The first needs only columns the index carries, so it reads 8 pages. The second needs column v, so it must visit the heap, and because the matching rows are physically scattered those 1000 rows live on 1000 distinct pages: 1000 random reads instead of 8. The cost of a covering index is write amplification and space, since every added column is maintained on every update. INCLUDE is the refinement: key columns are stored in internal nodes too, so a wide payload in the key would cut fanout, while INCLUDE keeps it in leaves.

L4.prompt_tpl: A query matches {rows} rows through an index. The rows are randomly scattered over a {pages}-page heap. Estimate heap page reads with and without a covering index, and state the ratio. Answer with the expected heap page reads without a covering index.
L4.answer: Without covering: expected distinct pages touched = pages * (1 - (1 - 1/pages)^rows). For rows=1000, pages=8334: 8334*(1-(1-1/8334)^1000) = 8334*0.1132 = 943. For rows=1000, pages=100000: 995. For rows=100, pages=8334: 99.4. For rows=100, pages=100000: 99.95. With covering: 0 heap pages. The measured Postgres case reported exactly 1000 heap blocks for 1000 rows on an 8334-page heap, close to the 943 the birthday-style estimate predicts.
L4.explanation: The estimate matters because it tells you when a covering index is worth it: when matched rows are far fewer than heap pages, nearly every row costs its own random read, so covering removes almost all the I/O. When matched rows greatly exceed heap pages a sequential scan was going to win anyway.

L4.prompt_tpl: An index-only scan works in staging but shows `Heap Fetches: {hf}` and runs slowly in production, on an identical schema. Give the cause and the fix.
L4.answer: The production table is written to constantly, so many pages are not marked all-visible in the visibility map and the engine must fetch each such row from the heap to check visibility. Staging is static and fully vacuumed. The fix is more aggressive autovacuum on that table, since only VACUUM sets visibility-map bits; there is no way to get a true index-only scan on pages with recent writes.
L4.explanation: This is a Postgres-specific consequence of storing visibility in the heap rather than in the index. InnoDB and SQL Server do not have it, because their indexes can answer visibility questions from undo or from the row itself.

prereqs: B+ tree fanout and height arithmetic

concepts.t: The LSM read path: memtable, SSTables, bloom filters
concepts.L1: An LSM engine buffers writes in a sorted in-memory memtable, flushes it whole as an immutable sorted file, and merges those files in the background. Reads must consult every run that could hold the key, newest first.
concepts.L2: Bloom filters make point lookups cheap and do nothing for range scans, because a range has no single key to test. That asymmetry is the real reason LSM engines lose to B-trees on scan-heavy workloads, more than compaction cost.
concepts.L3: The write path is fast because it is a memory insert plus a sequential log append, so a random-key workload costs no random I/O at write time. The bill arrives at read time and at compaction time. A point read walks the memtables, then every L0 file (their ranges overlap, so none can be skipped), then at most one file per deeper level. With m runs and no filters that is m index lookups; at 10 bits per key roughly 0.8 percent of negative probes proceed to read a block, so the expected cost collapses to about one real lookup. A range scan must open an iterator on every run and merge them, so its cost is proportional to the number of runs regardless of filters.

L4.prompt_tpl: An LSM has {runs} sorted runs that could hold a key. Each run has a bloom filter with a {fpr} false-positive rate. For a key that is absent, what is the expected number of runs whose data block is actually read?
L4.answer: Expected block reads = runs * fpr. For runs=12, fpr=0.008: 0.096. For runs=12, fpr=0.01: 0.12. For runs=40, fpr=0.008: 0.32. For runs=40, fpr=0.01: 0.40. Without filters it would be runs, i.e. 12 or 40. A range scan gets none of this benefit and pays all 12 or 40 iterator opens.
L4.explanation: This is why bloom filters are non-negotiable in LSM engines and why tiered compaction, which multiplies the number of runs, remains viable for point-lookup workloads but not for scans.

L4.prompt_tpl: A table is loaded, then 90 percent of its rows are deleted, and a range scan over the remaining rows becomes far slower than before the load. Explain in terms of the LSM read path.
L4.answer: Deletes in an LSM write tombstones rather than removing data. A range scan must iterate every run, read every tombstone in the range, and discard the shadowed keys, so it does roughly the work of scanning the pre-delete data set. The space and the cost are only reclaimed when compaction merges those levels and drops the tombstones, which for the deepest level may not happen for a long time.
L4.explanation: Cassandra's tombstone_failure_threshold exists for exactly this, and RocksDB offers DeleteRange to write one range tombstone instead of millions of point tombstones.

concepts.t: NVMe and the assumptions it broke

L0.body:
# The hardware constants a storage engine is tuned against.
#                  random 4K read   sequential BW   queue depth
# 15k SAS disk        ~200 IOPS        ~150 MB/s        1
# SATA SSD         ~90,000 IOPS        ~550 MB/s       32
# NVMe PCIe4    ~1,000,000 IOPS      ~7,000 MB/s   65535 queues

# PostgreSQL 16 still ships defaults that encode the first row:
SHOW seq_page_cost;             -- 1
SHOW random_page_cost;          -- 4   (says random is 4x dearer)
SHOW effective_io_concurrency;  -- 1   (measured)

# On NVMe the true ratio is closer to 1.1:1.
L0.cloze:
-- The old model: one seek dominates everything, so minimise {{c1::random}}
-- I/O and read sequentially even if you read more bytes.
-- NVMe changes three constants: latency falls to microseconds, random and
-- sequential throughput nearly {{c2::converge}}, and the device needs deep
-- {{c3::parallelism}} to reach its rated numbers.
-- Practical consequences: lower {{c4::random_page_cost}} toward 1.1,
-- raise effective_io_concurrency, and expect the {{c5::CPU}} rather than
-- the disk to become the bottleneck.

concepts.L1: NVMe replaced one shallow command queue over a bus designed for rotating disks with up to 65535 queues of 65536 commands each, straight onto PCIe. Random 4K reads went from hundreds per second to about a million, and latency from milliseconds to tens of microseconds.
concepts.L2: The engines did not automatically follow. PostgreSQL's random_page_cost of 4 and MySQL's default I/O capacity encode 2005 hardware, so on NVMe the planner systematically over-values sequential scans and under-uses indexes until someone changes the constant.
concepts.L3: Every classic storage-engine decision was made against a cost model where one random seek cost about 10 milliseconds and sequential bandwidth was free by comparison. That justified large pages, aggressive read-ahead, sorting to turn random access into sequential, and the LSM argument that trading write amplification for sequential writes is worth it. NVMe weakens all of them: random and sequential throughput converge, so the LSM trade buys less while write amplification still burns finite flash endurance. The subtler change is that a device needing queue depth 64 for its rated IOPS gets nothing from a single-threaded engine, which is why prefetching and io_uring became database features.

L4.prompt_tpl: A query must read {pages} randomly located 8 KB pages. Compute the time on a device delivering {iops} random IOPS at queue depth 1, then the time if the engine can keep {qd} requests in flight on a device whose per-request latency is 80 microseconds. Answer with the serial time in seconds at queue depth 1.
L4.answer: Serial time = pages / iops. For pages=10000, iops=200: 50 s. For pages=10000, iops=500000: 0.02 s. For pages=1000, iops=200: 5 s. For pages=1000, iops=500000: 0.002 s. With queue depth qd and 80 us latency, time = pages * 80e-6 / qd: for pages=10000, qd=32: 0.025 s; qd=64: 0.0125 s. The point: at qd=1 the 80 us latency caps you at 12500 IOPS no matter what the device can do.
L4.explanation: Latency times concurrency is the throughput ceiling. A device rated for a million IOPS delivers 12500 to a single-threaded reader, which is why effective_io_concurrency and prefetching matter more than the device spec sheet.

L4.prompt_tpl: A PostgreSQL instance moves from spinning disks to NVMe. The team reports that large queries still choose sequential scans where an index would now be faster. Name the single setting most likely responsible and the value to try, and say what evidence would confirm it.
L4.answer: random_page_cost, still at its default of 4. On NVMe the real ratio to seq_page_cost is close to 1.1, so set random_page_cost to about 1.1. Confirm by running the query with `SET random_page_cost = 1.1` in the session and checking that the plan flips to an index scan and that measured EXPLAIN ANALYZE time improves; also raise effective_io_concurrency so bitmap heap scans can prefetch.
L4.explanation: Change it per session and measure before making it global. effective_cache_size is the other commonly stale setting: it should reflect total RAM available for caching, not shared_buffers alone.

prereqs: B+ tree fanout and height arithmetic

L0.body:
Read overhead R, Update overhead U, Memory (space) overhead M.
Athanassoulis et al., EDBT 2016: minimise any two, the third rises.

  B+ tree    R ~ log_f(N) page reads   U ~ in-place write + WAL
             M ~ 1.4x data (69% fill)     -> good R and M, worse U
  LSM tree   R ~ runs consulted        U ~ one memory write, amortised
             M ~ 1.1x (levelled)          -> good U, worse R
  Hash index R ~ 1                     U ~ 1
   in memory M ~ 3-10x data               -> good R and U, bad M

Adaptive designs move along the surface; they do not leave it.
L0.cloze:
The three overheads are {{c1::read}}, {{c2::update}} and {{c3::memory}}.
Optimise any two and the {{c4::third}} degrades.
B+ trees give up {{c5::update}} cost; LSM trees give up read cost;
in-memory indexes give up space.

concepts.L1: Read overhead, update overhead, and memory overhead form a triangle. Optimizing two comes at the cost of the third.
concepts.L2: This is the cleanest available framing for storage engine choice and almost nobody cites it. B-trees optimize read and space; LSM trees optimize write; in-memory indexes optimize read and write at the cost of space.
concepts.L3: The conjecture converts a taste argument into a placement question: name the two overheads your workload cannot afford and the structure follows. It also predicts the escape hatches. Bloom filters buy read overhead back for an LSM by spending memory. Covering indexes buy it back for a B+ tree by spending space and update cost. Compression buys space by spending CPU, a fourth axis the conjecture does not model, which is why column stores appear to cheat. When someone claims a structure better on all three, the honest reading is that they changed the workload assumption - usually to read-mostly, or to a key distribution where most probes are negative.

L4.prompt_tpl: A workload does {w} writes per second and {r} point reads per second on a data set far larger than RAM, with a strict space budget. Name the structure the RUM conjecture points at and the overhead you are consciously accepting.
L4.answer: For 200000 writes and 1000 reads: an LSM tree, accepting read overhead, since reads must consult several runs. For 1000 writes and 200000 reads: a B+ tree, accepting update overhead, since each write is a random in-place page write plus WAL. In both cases the space budget rules out an in-memory hash index, which is the structure that would otherwise serve both.
L4.explanation: The conjecture's value is forcing the third overhead to be named out loud. The follow-up question is always which of the escape hatches (bloom filters, covering indexes, compression) buys back the one you gave up.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone argues that adding a bloom filter to an LSM tree disproves the RUM conjecture, because reads got cheaper with no cost to writes. Rebut it in two sentences.
L4.answer: The bloom filter is paid for in memory: roughly 10 bits per key, held resident, which is precisely the M axis. It trades along the surface rather than escaping it, and the trade is a good one only because the memory cost per key is far smaller than the data it lets you avoid reading.
L4.explanation: The same reasoning applies to every apparent counterexample. Ask which resource the improvement consumes; there is always one, and naming it is the skill the conjecture is teaching.

prereqs: B+ tree fanout and height arithmetic
